title: Wrap-Up Check
description: Twenty quick questions to lock in what you built today — about five minutes. No score pressure: this is a recap, not an exam.

intake.notesPlaceholder: Follow up on anything you flagged during the Try-it.
intake.lead: No results from this Check are sent anywhere — your answers stay on this machine. The short form is for anyone who would like further information on Pentaho: fill it in only if you want us to follow up, otherwise leave it blank and start.

questions.prompt: You want to inspect the data mid-pipeline, after the filter but before anything is written. In PDI you...
options: Right-click the step and Preview — at any step, at any time
Add temporary logging code and re-deploy
Run the whole pipeline and query the target table
Export the stream to CSV and open it in Excel
questions.explanation: Preview works on every step while you build — the habit from Lab 1. You inspect the stream before anything is committed anywhere.

questions.prompt: How did the columns and types of the sales CSV get defined in your transformation?
options: Get Fields read the file and proposed the schema, which you could then correct
You wrote a schema file by hand first
PDI requires the source team to supply an XSD
Columns are always read as strings and cast later in SQL
questions.explanation: Get Fields infers names, types and formats from the data itself — and the grid lets you fix anything it guessed wrong. It's also why Lab 6 worked on a file PDI had never seen.

questions.prompt: In Lab 3 you brought together CSV sales, a JSON customer master, a product catalogue and a region reference. What staging was required first?
options: None — the streams were looked up and joined on the canvas as they flowed
All three files had to be loaded into MySQL first
The JSON had to be converted to CSV outside the tool
A schema registry entry for each source
questions.explanation: Stream lookup and Merge join both work on rows in flight — Stream lookup holds a small reference set in memory, Merge join streams two sorted inputs with full inner/outer semantics. Format differences disappear at the Input step; after that, everything is rows.

questions.prompt: After you changed customer C001's region and re-ran the load, the dimension table showed...
options: Two rows for C001 — the old region with its validity window closed, the new one open-ended
One updated row for C001 — the old region was overwritten
A constraint violation on the natural key
Twenty-one new rows — the whole file was reloaded
questions.explanation: That's a Type 2 slowly changing dimension: Dimension lookup/update versioned the changed record and left the other nineteen untouched — the behaviour that normally costs a page of hand-written MERGE SQL.
questions.source: Lab 4 — Track History with One Step

questions.prompt: In Lab 5, onboarding the fourth feed (the Scotland file) required...
options: Adding one row to control.csv — no pipeline was opened
Copying the template and editing its reader for the new file
A new transformation per feed, as usual
Regenerating the template from the driver
questions.explanation: Metadata injection turns pipeline configuration into data. The template stays untouched; the control file — which an operations team can own — defines the feeds.

questions.prompt: Which of these does moving from today's Developer Edition lab to a production deployment add? Select all that apply.
options: Scheduled, monitored execution on a server instead of a laptop designer
Clustered / scaled-out execution
A commercial licence covering production use, with support
A different pipeline format — today's transformations must be rebuilt
questions.explanation: Everything you built today is real PDI and moves to production as-is — what the platform adds is the operational layer (scheduling, monitoring, scale-out, governance) and the licence and support to run it in production.

questions.prompt: In Lab 2, what happened to the sales rows that failed validation?
options: They were routed down a reject stream and written to a file for the source team
The transformation stopped with an error on the first bad row
They were silently dropped
They were fixed automatically by the filter step
questions.explanation: Bad data is a routing decision, not a crash: the Filter rows FALSE branch carried the rejects to their own output, while the valid rows continued — visible on the canvas, no try/except code.

questions.prompt: Beyond the local files used today, where can PDI's Input steps read from?
options: Databases, Excel, cloud storage (S3), HTTP and other VFS locations — the same canvas pattern
Local CSV and text files only
Only sources that have a JDBC driver
Anything, but each source needs custom plugin development first
questions.explanation: The pattern you learned generalises: swap the Input step and the rest of the pipeline is unchanged — databases, spreadsheets, cloud object storage, APIs and message queues are all first-class sources.

questions.prompt: In production, what sequences your transformations, retries failures, and alerts someone when the source file doesn't arrive?
options: A job (.kjb), scheduled and monitored on a server
A cron script that calls each transformation in order
Each transformation schedules itself
The Filter rows step
questions.explanation: Jobs are the orchestration layer: success/failure routing between entries, retries, notifications — and a server runs them on schedule with logging and history.

questions.prompt: What does the Pentaho Developer Edition licence (BSL 1.1) cover?
options: Evaluation, development, and learning — production use requires a commercial licence
Any use, including production, free of charge
A 30-day time-limited trial that then stops working
Non-commercial personal use only
questions.explanation: Developer Edition is the full product for evaluating and building — it doesn't expire. Running it in production is what needs the commercial licence (which also brings support and certified updates).

questions.prompt: In Lab 2 you hopped Filter rows to Text file output and PDI asked which result to send. Rows that fail the condition travel down...
options: The FALSE hop, to whichever step you connected it to
The same hop as valid rows, flagged with an extra column
Nowhere — failing rows are discarded unless you add error handling
Back to the input step to be re-read
questions.explanation: Filter rows has two real output hops. TRUE and FALSE are separate streams, each with its own downstream step and thread — which is why you could preview the rejects on their own in Lab 1.

questions.prompt: After Get Fields, what does the Text file input step hold besides the file path?
options: Row metadata — each column's name, type and format — which travels down the hops ahead of the data
A cached copy of the whole file
A generated Java class that parses the file
Nothing — types are only decided when the row is written
questions.explanation: Row metadata is why the next step already knows unit_price is a Number and order_date is a Date, and why a mis-typed column is caught at design time rather than at run time.

questions.prompt: When you ran the four-step transformation in Lab 2, how did the steps execute?
options: All at once — each step on its own thread, rows flowing between them through small buffers
One after another — the reader finished, then the filter ran, then the outputs
In the order you dragged them onto the canvas
Only the input step runs; the others are applied when rows are written
questions.explanation: The filter was already working on row 1 while the reader parsed row 20. Only the rows in flight are held in memory, which is why the same design handles files far larger than RAM.

questions.prompt: What is a .ktr file?
options: XML describing the steps, their settings and the hops — the engine executes it directly
Compiled bytecode generated from the canvas
A binary snapshot of the last run
A shortcut to a transformation stored inside the server database
questions.explanation: No code is generated: the dialog reads and writes the XML, and the same file is what the server runs. That is also why a .ktr diffs and merges in git like source code.

questions.prompt: Which situation calls for a Merge join rather than a Stream lookup?
options: You need outer-join semantics, or a key may legitimately match many rows, or neither side fits in memory
The reference set is a small, stable code table
You want exactly one value per row, fast
The lookup data comes from JSON rather than CSV
questions.explanation: Stream lookup holds the whole lookup stream in RAM and returns at most one match per row. Merge join streams both sides, supports INNER / LEFT / RIGHT / FULL OUTER, and can multiply rows — at the price of sorted input.

questions.prompt: Why did the Merge join in Lab 3 need two Sort rows steps in front of it?
options: Merge join walks both streams in lock-step, so each must already be ordered by its join keys
Sort rows removes duplicate keys before joining
PDI cannot read two files at once without sorting them
The output file has to be in region order
questions.explanation: Merge join holds only the current row from each side and advances whichever is behind. Unsorted input does not raise an error — it silently walks past matches it can no longer see.

questions.prompt: The region join was configured as LEFT OUTER. What does that protect against?
options: A sale whose region code is missing from regions.csv silently disappearing from the output
Duplicate region rows multiplying sales
The region file being read before the sales file
Null values in the manager_email column
questions.explanation: INNER would drop any sale with no matching region. LEFT OUTER keeps every sale and leaves the region columns empty — the difference between "some sales went missing" and "some sales need a region added".

questions.prompt: In the Calculator step, why does the guide insist on unit_price × qty rather than qty × unit_price?
options: The calculation runs in Field A's data type, so an Integer in A rounds the price to a whole number before multiplying
Field A must always be the larger number
qty is a String until it is placed in Field B
It makes no difference — the two orders give the same result
questions.explanation: 2 × 49.99 came out as 100.0 with qty first. Putting the decimal field in A keeps the pennies — a small rule with an expensive failure mode.

questions.prompt: After the first Lab 4 load, dim_customer held 21 rows for 20 customers. Where did the extra row come from?
options: Dimension lookup/update inserts a technical "unknown" member (key 0) so later loads can point failed lookups somewhere
One customer appeared twice in customers.json
The header row of the JSON was loaded as data
A test row you added when you clicked SQL
questions.explanation: The unknown row is deliberate warehouse hygiene: a fact row whose customer cannot be found is attached to key 0 instead of being dropped or failing the load.
questions.source: Lab 4 — Track History with One Step

questions.prompt: Why does the Lab 5 driver job run the injector transformation once per control-file row, instead of once for all feeds?
options: One metadata-injection run fills the template with one configuration, so three differently-delimited feeds need three runs
The template can only read files under 1 MB
Jobs cannot pass more than one row to a transformation
Each feed has to be sorted before injection
questions.explanation: Injection rewrites the template in memory with the values you mapped — one filename, one separator — and executes that copy. "Execute for every input row" supplies the loop, and Get rows from result is where each control row arrives.
